claim: Nobody has published, for a general audience, an account of what specific evidence would actually settle whether social media harms adolescents — naming the study designs capable of resolving it, which of those have been run, and why the remainder have not.
counterexample: Multiple general-audience publications explicitly name the study designs capable of resolving the causal question, survey which have been run, and explain why the remainder have not. The strongest single counterexample is the 2024 National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine report 'Social Media and Adolescent Health' (freely readable at NAP.edu/NCBI Bookshelf), which in its Research chapter names RCTs, natural experiments, and longitudinal designs; reviews which have been run (e.g., Allcott et al. 2019 deactivation RCT, Braghieri et al. 2022 Facebook rollout natural experiment); and explains why the remainder have not been run — they are 'difficult and expensive to conduct' and require platform algorithm access that platforms do not grant independent researchers. A second counterexample is Chris Felton's May 2026 arXiv preprint 'Notes on Randomized Controlled Trials for Studying Social Media Harms' (arXiv:2606.00900), which is written accessibly, names the local-vs-global RCT distinction as the key gap, explains why existing RCTs fail to test the social media hypothesis, and describes what an adequate trial would look like. A third is the August 2026 Knowable Magazine piece 'What can we learn from Australia's social media ban for teens?' which names longitudinal studies, natural experiments, and cluster-randomized designs, states which have been run and found inconclusive, and explains why the remainder have not — the methodological crisis stems from social media's complexity as a networked ecosystem that confounds conventional designs.

quote: "rigorous study designs that would shed light on the extent to which social media causes harms are severely lacking"
why_it_still_matters: This breaks the sentence entirely, not merely its framing. The claim is a universal negative ('nobody has published') and at least three general-audience or general-readership publications — the National Academies report (widely covered in mainstream press), the Knowable Magazine article, and the Felton arXiv preprint (cited in popular debate) — each do exactly what the sentence says nobody has done: they name specific study designs, report which have been run, and explain why the remainder have not. The sentence's conclusion — that this gap in the public discourse exists — is false. The underlying policy concern (that the evidence base is weak) may still be valid, but the specific claim about the absence of a published account is not.
inherited_from: The claim appears to be an original assertion rather than a restatement of a narrower source claim. However, it may echo a rhetorical move common in op-eds and advocacy pieces (e.g., Haidt/Rausch's After Babel Substack) that frame the debate as lacking a clear evidentiary roadmap — but those pieces themselves partially provide such a roadmap, further undermining the universal claim.

claim: The studies capable of resolving the causal question can be run using data available to independent researchers, without access to platform-held exposure and content data.
counterexample: The claim is false for the class of studies most capable of resolving the causal question — specifically, studies of platform algorithm effects and content-exposure effects. Multiple sources establish that (a) the studies most capable of resolving causality require platform-held data or platform collaboration, and (b) independent researchers have developed workarounds precisely because they lack that access, but those workarounds are acknowledged to be second-best. However, the claim is also partially broken in the opposite direction: a growing body of work shows that some causal designs — deactivation RCTs, natural experiments using policy rollouts (e.g., Australia's ban), and independent research platforms using AI bots — can be run without platform data. The Piccardi et al. (2025, Science) 'platform-independent experiments' paradigm uses browser extensions and LLMs to rerank feeds without platform collaboration. The Felton (2026) arXiv paper and the Knowable Magazine (2026) piece both identify the Australia ban as a natural experiment that independent researchers can study without platform data. So the claim is BROKEN in both directions: it is too strong when it implies ALL causal designs require platform data (deactivation RCTs and natural experiments do not), and it is also wrong when applied to the most powerful designs (algorithm/content studies do require platform data or collaboration).

quote: "Conducting a real-world experiment on the causal effects of platform features generally requires the collaboration of the platform being studied, which rarely happens"
why_it_still_matters: This breaks the sentence in a way that matters substantively for the piece's conclusion. If the piece is arguing that independent researchers are sufficient to resolve the causal question, that is wrong for the most important class of studies (algorithm/content effects). If the piece is arguing that platform data is always necessary, that is also wrong — deactivation RCTs, natural experiments (Australia ban, Facebook rollout), and independent research platforms (Piccardi et al.; the AI-bot platform in arXiv:2601.16040) can all generate causal evidence without platform-held data. The correct, narrower claim is: studies of platform-level algorithm and content-exposure effects require platform collaboration or data, while studies of use-level effects (deactivation, restriction) can be run independently. The sentence as written collapses this distinction and is false in both directions.
inherited_from: This claim may be inherited from a common rhetorical move in the 'open up platform data' advocacy literature (e.g., National Academies Chapter 8, which calls for facilitating independent research on platform algorithms). That literature's actual, narrower claim is that algorithm-specific causal research requires platform data — not that all causal research does. The scope was dropped when the claim was generalized.
